newsitem.title: USA: First jurors called in Oklahoma City bomb case.
newsitem.headline: First jurors called in Oklahoma City bomb case.

text.p: The Oklahoma City bombing trial began on Monday with Timothy McVeigh, the man accused of planting the bomb that killed 168 people nearly two years ago, appearing relaxed at the start of jury selection.

The process could take weeks since finding impartial jurors amid the massive pretrial publicity will likely be difficult for both sides. The first potential juror admitted he had heard about media reports that McVeigh confessed to planting the bomb outside the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, although the potential juror said it would not affect his judgment.
McVeigh's lawyers have denied the report of a confession.

McVeigh officially was on trial for the "use of a weapon of mass destruction" and the murder of eight federal officials. A second defendant, his former Army buddy Terry Nichols, will be tried separately on charges resulting from the worst bombing in U.S. history. No date has been set for that trial.

McVeigh, wearing a blue shirt, khaki pants and military-style crew cut, smiled periodically during the morning session, even though he faces the death penalty if found guilty. He followed the proceedings intensely and took notes on a yellow legal pad.
Three marshals sat behind him in one of many signs of intense security. The federal courthouse in downtown Denver was ringed by concrete barriers and surveillance cameras swept the sidewalks.

Trash cans were removed and replaced by clear plastic bags and manhole covers were sealed. Courtroom visitors had to go through metal detectors and show picture identification. Police and bomb-sniffing dogs patrolled the area.

Prospective jurors were called by U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch from a pool of 1,000 people who filled in a 40-page questionnaire on every aspect of their background and opinions about the case. By lunchtime only two had been interviewed.

The first prospective juror, who was shielded from public view by a courtroom screen, said he knew about mixing explosives and thought there was government "overkill" in the Branch Davidian siege in Waco, Texas, that killed some 80 people in 1993, an event the prosecution said McVeigh wanted to avenge.

The man, a self-employed investment adviser with a mining background, described himself as "a normal human being" who had been deeply saddened by the Oklahoma City tragedy. Identified only as juror 858, he admitted knowing about press reports that McVeigh told his lawyers of planting the bomb but said he quickly turned away from the radio when the story came on.
Defence attorney Stephen Jones had unsuccessfully asked for a delay in the trial claiming the press reports had tainted the 28-year-old Gulf War veteran's chances of receiving a fair trial.

The potential juror said he would not be influenced by the reports, adding: "It's not the first time that the press was wrong and not the last time. They want to sell their broadcasts and newspapers ... I don't know if they are wrong, I don't know if they are right."

The second juror, a grandmother of four children who said she loved Western novels, said she felt sorry for McVeigh when she saw a photograph of him shortly after his arrest. "I felt very sorry for such a young man to have wasted his life," she said when Jones demanded to know what she meant. "If he's found guilty, he has wasted his life."

A tense-looking William McVeigh, the defendant's father, was in court, where 12 seats were also set aside for the survivors and family members of those killed. Roy Sells, whose wife Lee died in the bombing, was up at dawn to get a courtroom seat.
"I want to see who they eliminate and who they choose," he said of the jurors.

Tom Kight, whose stepdaughter Frankie Merrell, 23, died in the blast, said the family was still haunted by her loss. "Yesterday was a difficult day because it was Easter. We were recalling hiding Easter eggs when Frankie was small," he said.
In Oklahoma City, a closed-circuit telecast was beamed to a Federal Aviation Administration facility where survivors and family of the victims could see the proceedings.
